title: When not to use a model
definition: Solving a task with explicit rules, forms, search, or conventional software when generative output is unnecessary.
example: Validate an expense claim against a published reimbursement policy using a form and deterministic rules.
nuance: Compare an exact allowance calculation with an ambiguous business-purpose description; only the latter may need interpretation.
evidence: Boundary-value tests and an explicit needs-review result for ambiguous cases; compare with a scripted model mistake.

title: Chat
definition: A conversational interface in which a person supplies messages and decides what to do with the replies.
example: Ask for help drafting an invitation to a neighborhood repair workshop.
nuance: Contrast a useful draft with an invented venue detail; the conversation has no implicit access to your calendar or facts.
evidence: A checked facts list and a revised draft grounded in information the user actually provided.

title: Prompt engineering
definition: Designing instructions, examples, and output expectations to steer a model's response.
example: Turn a vague request for a workshop announcement into a brief with audience, facts, tone, and length.
nuance: Change one instruction at a time; stronger wording cannot supply absent facts or guarantee compliance.
evidence: A rubric comparing factual fidelity, audience fit, and constraints across clearly labeled sample outputs.

title: Structured output
definition: Constraining an answer to a defined data structure so software can validate and consume it.
example: Extract an event date, venue, and accessibility information from an organizer's email into a registration form.
nuance: A valid structure may contain wrong facts; missing values need an explicit unknown state instead of invention.
evidence: Show the friendly form first, optional JSON second, schema validation, and field-by-field source evidence.

title: Reasoning at answer time
definition: Allocating additional inference computation to work through a problem before returning an answer.
example: Schedule workshop sessions around room, trainer, and equipment constraints.
nuance: More computation does not ensure correctness; do not present invented hidden reasoning as a real model trace.
evidence: An observable candidate schedule, constraint checker, counterexample, and labeled illustrative cost/quality comparison.

title: Images, audio and video
definition: Working with inputs or outputs across text, images, audio, or video.
example: Create an equipment intake record from a label photo and a technician's voice note.
nuance: Blur a serial number and introduce disagreement between image and audio; ask for confirmation instead of asserting certainty.
evidence: Highlighted source regions, transcript excerpts, uncertain fields, and a corrected intake record.

title: Context engineering
definition: Selecting and arranging the instructions, reference material, and history included in each model request.
example: Prepare a support reply using the current product manual, customer question, and relevant case history.
nuance: Compare a relevant excerpt with a stale manual and distracting history; context size is not context quality.
evidence: A visible request-context tray, version labels, included/excluded evidence, and answer differences.

title: Embeddings and search
definition: Representing content numerically and retrieving similar items, often combined with keyword or metadata search.
example: Find the right troubleshooting article for a customer who says the machine makes a knocking sound.
nuance: Contrast semantic similarity with an exact model-number lookup; a similar passage may refer to the wrong product.
evidence: Ranked snippets, model filters, relevance judgments, and a case where hybrid search is preferable.

title: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
definition: Retrieving external information and placing it in the model's context to support an answer.
example: Answer an appliance warranty question from a small versioned document collection.
nuance: Include a missing exclusion clause and conflicting revisions; retrieval and generation can fail separately.
evidence: Visible query, retrieved passages, grounded answer, source links, and an abstention when evidence is insufficient.

title: Knowledge graphs and GraphRAG
definition: Representing entities and relationships explicitly; GraphRAG uses graph-based retrieval or summaries to support generation.
example: Trace which shipped products depend on a recalled supplier component across purchase and assembly records.
nuance: Contrast an ordinary document search with a multi-hop dependency question; uncertain or missing edges must remain visible.
evidence: A provenance-linked path from supplier to lot to product, a missing-edge case, and a checked affected-product list.

title: Memory
definition: Persisting selected information across interactions and retrieving it when relevant.
example: A workshop planning assistant remembers the user's preferred meeting times between sessions.
nuance: Separate an explicit preference from a one-time exception; stale memories must be editable or deletable.
evidence: A memory card with origin, update, removal, and a new-session test showing what was actually loaded.

title: Prompt chaining
definition: Running model calls in a predetermined sequence where one step's output feeds the next.
example: Draft a weekly portfolio status report through fixed stages: collect current evidence, reconcile it, build project summaries, then assemble the report.
nuance: An extraction error can become a polished false claim downstream; previous reports supply continuity, not proof of current status.
evidence: A source-linked evidence sheet, intermediate project summaries, report diff, and a corrected unsupported claim.

title: Routing
definition: Selecting a handler or workflow based on an input's category, rules, or classification.
example: Send incoming support messages to billing, troubleshooting, or a human escalation queue.
nuance: Mixed intent and low confidence require explicit handling; a route choice does not resolve the underlying issue.
evidence: A routing decision, confidence limitation, mixed-intent case, and a confusion matrix on labeled sample messages.

title: Parallel calls
definition: Running independent tasks concurrently and combining their outputs.
example: Collect and summarize current status for several projects independently before composing one weekly portfolio report.
nuance: Project-specific work can run concurrently, but stale sources and inconsistent milestone dates require reconciliation before aggregation.
evidence: Per-project evidence cards, timestamps, conflicting-source flags, and a combined report with no invented update for silent projects.

title: Write and check
definition: Iterating between generating a candidate and evaluating it against criteria until it passes or a limit stops the loop.
example: Revise an onboarding article against a factual and readability checklist.
nuance: A reviewer can miss errors or reward superficial fixes; repeated polishing may never converge.
evidence: Draft diffs, criterion-level feedback, a maximum-attempt stop, and an independent source check.

title: Workflow graphs
definition: Representing a predetermined process as steps, transitions, branches, and persistent state.
example: Generate a weekly multi-project status report from prior reports and current trackers, notes, and milestones, then route the draft for human review.
nuance: Missing data, connector failures, edits after approval, and send retries need separate states; a scheduled fixed workflow is not automatically an autonomous agent.
evidence: A collection-to-review state graph, evidence links, unresolved-items queue, version-bound approval, and simulated duplicate-safe delivery.

title: Human approval
definition: Pausing a process for a person's scoped approval, correction, or decision.
example: Review and approve the exact weekly status report and recipient list before the application sends it.
nuance: Reject or edit the draft; any change to approved content or recipients requires renewed approval. No response means no send.
evidence: A previous-versus-current diff, evidence inspection, approve/edit/reject decisions, and a clearly simulated delivery record.

title: Function calling
definition: A model proposing a named tool and structured arguments that application code validates and executes.
example: Ask an assistant to check stock and prepare a reservation for replacement parts.
nuance: A tool call is a proposal, not authorization; handle invalid arguments, absent stock, and tool failure.
evidence: English request, optional argument view, validation result, read-only lookup, and a separately approved reservation.

title: Code execution
definition: Running generated code in a constrained environment to perform computation or transform data.
example: Analyze a CSV of energy readings and produce daily totals and a chart.
nuance: Malformed timestamps, missing rows, and unit mismatches affect results; a sandbox bounds access but does not ensure correct math.
evidence: Input preview, inspectable Python, deterministic totals, a planted unit error, and denied file/network access in a mock boundary demonstration.

title: Model Context Protocol
definition: A protocol for exposing tools, resources, and other capabilities to compatible AI applications.
example: Connect an assistant to a mock inventory service and an internal manual resource.
nuance: Discovery is not permission; tool descriptions can be misleading and services can be unavailable.
evidence: Capability discovery, a tool request/result, access refusal, and an outage, clearly separated from transport details.

title: Computer and browser use
definition: An agent observing and interacting with a graphical interface through actions such as clicks and typing.
example: Complete a mock equipment return form in a browser portal with no API.
nuance: A layout change or stale screen can invalidate a click; submission requires a final review.
evidence: Screen/action/result sequence, mistaken-field recovery, and a simulated confirmation with no external transaction.

title: Single agent
definition: A model choosing successive actions and when to stop within a tool-enabled loop.
example: Investigate why a room-booking request failed using policy and availability tools.
nuance: Distinguish model-chosen next actions from a fixed chain; stop on insufficient evidence or a step cap.
evidence: Tool observations, changing next-step choices, a supported answer, and a bounded unsuccessful run.

title: The agent harness
definition: The runtime around an agent's model that manages tools, context, execution boundaries, approvals, limits, and records.
example: Generate a new DUT project using the shared Python test framework and the approved workflow.
nuance: Preserve separate approval for helpers and framework edits; no agent-operated instruments; syntax checks are not hardware validation.
evidence: The integrated DUT walkthrough, approved plan, file list, evidence/status record, missing-requirement case, and approval exercise.

title: Agentic RAG and deep research
definition: Retrieval where an agent chooses follow-up searches and reads until it can answer or must stop.
example: Investigate the same appliance warranty question when exclusions are split across documents.
nuance: Compare against one-pass RAG on the same evidence; repeated search can still miss facts or exceed its budget.
evidence: Search trajectory, evidence accumulated per step, citations, conflicts, and a stop/abstain case.

title: Coding agents
definition: Agents that inspect, edit, execute, and test code to complete a software task.
example: Fix a date-filter bug in a small event-registration application.
nuance: A passing test can miss regressions; keep edits scoped and distinguish simulated test logs from actually executed tests.
evidence: A reproducible failing case, reviewed patch, deterministic tests, edge-case regression, and change summary.

title: Skills
definition: Reusable task instructions and supporting resources loaded when an agent needs a particular procedure.
example: Produce a release note using an organization's writing and verification procedure.
nuance: A skill provides guidance rather than new permissions or guaranteed correctness; stale instructions can conflict with current policy.
evidence: Selected skill, loaded resources, draft release note, verification checklist, and outdated-skill handling.

title: Voice agents
definition: Agents that conduct spoken interactions while handling audio, timing, interruptions, and tool use.
example: Book a workshop place in a simulated spoken conversation.
nuance: Handle interruptions, an ambiguous date, and a misunderstood name; confirm before committing the booking.
evidence: Transcript/audio controls, turn state, correction, scoped confirmation, and a clearly simulated booking result.

title: Lead agent and workers
definition: A lead agent delegating bounded subtasks to workers and combining their results.
example: Prepare a venue comparison by assigning cost, transport, and accessibility research to separate workers.
nuance: Workers may duplicate work or return incompatible assumptions; delegation must have clear scope and evidence.
evidence: Task briefs, worker findings with sources, conflict resolution, and a consolidated recommendation without automatic purchase.

title: Agent graphs
definition: Representing agent roles and the permitted handoffs or transitions between them.
example: Triage a mock service incident through investigator, remediation planner, and reviewer roles.
nuance: A handoff carries state and authority boundaries; prevent endless cycles and uncontrolled privilege transfer.
evidence: Role graph, handoff packet, reviewer rejection, bounded retry, and a human-approved remediation plan.

title: Review and debate
definition: Using multiple model perspectives to critique or compare candidate answers before a decision.
example: Review two proposed data-retention policies for a fictional application against stated requirements.
nuance: Agreement is not independent evidence; reviewers can share errors or favor persuasive wording.
evidence: Claims linked to the supplied requirements, disagreements, adjudication, and a planted error both reviewers initially miss.

title: Long-running tasks
definition: Maintaining progress, state, and limits across an extended task or multiple sessions.
example: Migrate a fictional documentation site in batches with checkpoints.
nuance: A restart must preserve completed work and constraints; summaries can omit crucial decisions.
evidence: Task ledger, checkpoint, interrupted/resumed batch, stale-context case, and a budget-based partial handoff.

title: Always-on assistants
definition: Persistent assistants that act on configured triggers within ongoing responsibilities and permissions.
example: Prepare a weekly status-report draft on a schedule across active projects, then notify the responsible reviewer.
nuance: A trigger authorizes collection and drafting, not automatic distribution; handle time zones, missed runs, access limits, and duplicate drafts.
evidence: A simulated weekly trigger, run identifier, per-source collection record, waiting-for-review state, and one delivery only after explicit approval.

title: Organizations of agents
definition: Coordinating many agents with distinct responsibilities, shared resources, and organizational constraints.
example: Run a simulated product-launch preparation across research, documentation, support, and review teams.
nuance: More agents increase coordination costs and can spread bad assumptions; compare a smaller team baseline.
evidence: Dependency board, ownership, conflicting updates, shared budget, escalation, and an evidence-based launch readiness report.

title: Robots and machines
definition: Connecting model decisions to physical sensing and action through robot or machine control systems.
example: A simulated robot sorts labeled packages into bins.
nuance: Uncertain perception, unreachable objects, and emergency stops require explicit handling; simulation does not certify physical safety.
evidence: A 2D simulated scene, proposed action, constrained controller decision, uncertain-object stop, and a sim-to-real limitations note.

title: Evals
definition: Systematic measurement of performance against defined tasks, criteria, and reference judgments.
example: Compare two versions of a support assistant on a held-out set of customer questions.
nuance: Aggregate scores can hide critical failures; do not tune against the final test set or treat a model grader as ground truth.
evidence: Per-case outcomes, sliced metrics, disagreement review, uncertainty, and a documented ship/hold decision.

title: Evaluation frameworks
definition: Infrastructure for organizing datasets, executing runs, applying graders, and reporting evaluation results.
example: Build a small evaluation run for the same support assistant using recorded responses.
nuance: Missing cases, grading bugs, and inconsistent configurations can inflate scores.
evidence: Dataset version, reproducible run manifest, grader spot checks, failed-run accounting, and inspectable results.

title: Changing the model
definition: Choosing how to improve task performance through context, prompts, data, or changes to model weights.
example: Improve a support-message classifier that confuses two product categories.
nuance: Start with error analysis; distinguish retrieval/prompt changes from actual weight training and avoid assuming training is necessary.
evidence: A baseline error set, intervention comparison, held-out evaluation plan, and a justified choice of the simplest adequate method.

title: Fine-tuning and adapters
definition: Further training model weights, fully or through adapters, on task-specific examples.
example: Teach a classifier a stable internal support taxonomy using labeled historical messages.
nuance: Prevent train/test leakage and preserve rare categories; training is not a reliable store for frequently changing facts.
evidence: Dataset split, label audit, a clearly illustrative training artifact, and held-out before/after results only when real measurements exist.

title: Distillation
definition: Training a student model to approximate selected behavior of a teacher model.
example: Create a smaller support-label classifier from reviewed teacher-generated examples.
nuance: Teacher errors transfer to the student; lower cost can come with reduced coverage or calibration.
evidence: Teacher labels, human corrections, separate evaluation set, and a labeled illustrative quality/resource tradeoff.

title: Synthetic data
definition: Generating artificial examples for training or testing and checking their fitness for the intended use.
example: Expand rare support-message categories with generated examples.
nuance: Duplicates, unrealistic language, and label errors can make a dataset look larger without adding useful coverage.
evidence: Generation brief, accepted/rejected examples, diversity checks, and evaluation on independently collected real cases.

title: Prompt optimization
definition: Searching prompt variants against an objective using a development set.
example: Find a better extraction prompt for workshop registration emails.
nuance: Optimization can exploit the grader or overfit development examples; preserve an untouched test set.
evidence: Candidate prompts, development scores, a grader loophole, and final held-out comparison with versioned prompts.

title: Safety, privacy and governance
definition: Managing risks through data handling, permissions, consent, oversight, and accountable system design.
example: Design an assistant that summarizes confidential employee feedback for a fictional organization.
nuance: Useful summaries can still leak identity; access controls and retention obligations cannot be replaced by an instruction.
evidence: Data-flow map, minimization choices, access matrix, consent/retention assumptions, and an incident response exercise.

title: Guardrails
definition: Checks on inputs, outputs, or proposed actions that flag, block, or route problematic behavior.
example: An internal helpdesk assistant encounters a document requesting credential disclosure.
nuance: Separate untrusted content from instructions; classifiers can miss attacks or block legitimate requests, and filters are not sandboxes.
evidence: Input/action/output checks, a blocked request, false-positive review, and a permission boundary that remains independent.

title: Red teaming
definition: Deliberately probing a system for failures and turning findings into defenses and regression cases.
example: Attack the same mock helpdesk assistant with conflicting document instructions and unauthorized-data requests.
nuance: A finite set of attacks does not establish safety; retest defenses against variations and legitimate inputs.
evidence: Attack objective, observed failure, trace, mitigation, and a regression case with explicit scope.

title: Operations
definition: Deploying and maintaining an AI system with monitoring, versioning, incident response, and recovery.
example: Release a new support-assistant version to a simulated small traffic segment.
nuance: A quality regression can occur without a server error; plan rollback, capacity limits, and degraded operation.
evidence: Release manifest, staged rollout, quality alert, rollback event, and incident record.

title: Observability
definition: Recording the inputs, actions, decisions, and outcomes needed to understand a system's behavior.
example: Diagnose a wrong warranty answer caused by retrieval of an outdated manual.
nuance: Final-answer logs alone cannot identify the cause; logging also needs privacy controls.
evidence: Linked retrieval and model spans, document version, approval/stop records, redacted data, and a supported root-cause finding.

title: AI gateways
definition: A shared layer managing access, routing, policy, budgets, and telemetry across model services.
example: Route a helpdesk application's requests through a mock gateway when one provider times out.
nuance: Fallback can change behavior, privacy assumptions, and duplicate-request risk; compatibility is not guaranteed.
evidence: Route decision, timeout, allowed fallback, budget refusal, request identifier, and resulting quality check.

title: Cost optimization
definition: Reducing resource use or latency while preserving an explicitly defined level of quality.
example: Compare caching, shorter context, batching, and a smaller model for repeated support questions.
nuance: A cache can serve stale or unauthorized content; lower average cost can hide worse tail latency or errors.
evidence: Cache-hit/miss cases, scope/version keys, labeled sample costs, latency distribution, and a quality floor.

title: Running models locally
definition: Executing model inference on locally controlled hardware rather than a hosted model endpoint.
example: Choose a local document-summarization setup for an offline field laptop.
nuance: Model weights, context, and runtime overhead all consume memory; local execution alone does not guarantee private handling.
evidence: Clearly estimated memory budget, quantization comparison, offline data-flow review, and a benchmark plan without fabricated throughput.

title: Working with a model
definition: Practices for specifying, delegating, reviewing, and evaluating work done with a model.
example: Prepare an event proposal with the model as a drafting assistant and the organizer as accountable reviewer.
nuance: Quality depends on the entire collaboration cycle; confident prose is not verified work.
evidence: Task brief, delegation boundary, draft, independent checks, and a recorded acceptance decision.

title: Briefing: saying what you want
definition: Describing the goal, context, constraints, deliverables, and uncertainties so work can proceed without unnecessary guessing.
example: Ask for a community workshop plan with a budget, audience, venue constraints, and success criteria.
nuance: Show an incomplete brief, a clarification question, and a resolved assumption; avoid turning every detail into a rigid prescription.
evidence: Brief before/after, explicit unknowns, acceptance criteria, and a plan checked against them.

title: Reviewing work you did not do
definition: Independently checking another party's work before relying on or releasing it.
example: Review a model-written workshop budget and announcement.
nuance: Fluent writing can hide bad totals and invented facts; prioritize consequential errors rather than cosmetic edits.
evidence: Source-backed fact checks, recomputed totals, marked corrections, and a final review decision.

title: Deciding what to hand over
definition: Choosing which work a model may perform and which decisions or actions a person retains.
example: Split an event-organizing task into drafting, supplier comparison, booking, and payment.
nuance: Distinguish ability from authority; reversible drafts and consequential commitments need different boundaries.
evidence: Delegation matrix, permitted drafts, withheld transaction, and a change-of-scope approval case.

title: Calibrating trust
definition: Calibrating reliance on a model from observed performance in a particular task and context.
example: Track a drafting assistant across repeated event-planning tasks with varying difficulty.
nuance: Success on routine cases does not establish reliability on unusual ones; confidence and polished language are weak evidence.
evidence: A small labeled performance history, per-task review policy, a novel-case failure, and a justified change in oversight.

title: Graph engineering
definition: Distinguishing graphs of information from graphs that control workflows or agent handoffs.
example: Trace an equipment recall through a dependency graph, then process notifications through a workflow and agent review.
nuance: An edge meaning depends on the graph; knowing a dependency does not authorize a workflow action.
evidence: Three small linked graphs with explicit node/edge meanings and the same case followed across them.

title: Who approves what
definition: Tracing how human decision authority changes as more work becomes automated.
example: Follow a purchase from manually reviewed draft to bounded recurring replenishment.
nuance: Approval must attach to a specific action or policy; a past approval cannot silently expand scope.
evidence: An authority ladder, versioned approval records, an out-of-policy order, and an escalation decision.

title: Checking the work
definition: Matching verification methods to the kinds of errors a system can make.
example: Follow one wrong support answer from schema validation through evidence review and evaluation.
nuance: A well-formed answer can still be false; multiple agreeing agents can still repeat the same error.
evidence: Layered checks with the exact defect each detects, a remaining blind spot, and an appropriate human escalation.

title: What the model sees
definition: Tracing which information reaches each model request and why it was included.
example: Resume a support investigation after context compaction and a new conversation.
nuance: Saved memory or files do nothing unless loaded; instructions, retrieved documents, and tool results have different roles.
evidence: Before/after context trays, omitted evidence, restored constraints, and a corrected supported answer.
